To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) a spectral trajectory approach can be used to identify forest change; (2) the spectral trajectory approach is not as accurate as expected in the Pacific Northwest; (3) accuracy assessment is critical for the evaluation of automated change attribution methods; (4) a robust accuracy assessment is challenging; and (5) the spectral trajectory method does not perform well for insect disturbance and fire in Pacific Northwest forests.

(1) we found widespread disturbance within the negative NDVI anomalies, (2) the spectral trajectory method did not transfer well from other ecosystems and (3) we were unable to accurately attribute the cause of the decline in NDVI with Landsat data.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing and evaluating a new approach to map forest disturbance from Landsat time series data, with the ultimate goal of improving the accuracy of forest disturbance mapping.
understanding forest change in the Pacific Northwest, which has implications on carbon cycle modeling, forest management, and the development of remote sensing methods.
the transferability of automated methods for detecting and mapping forest disturbances.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the spectral trajectory method is not transferable to other ecosystems, and that the method needs to be modified to account for differences in ecosystem structure and disturbance regimes.
the spectral trajectory method is transferable to Pacific Northwest forests but that it does not perform with sufficient accuracy to attribute the decline to specific causal factors.
we were unable to find an automated LTSS method that accurately mapped fire and insect disturbance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the spectral trajectory method is not robust for mapping forest disturbance in the Pacific Northwest, but that it does provide information for multi year stress.
the LTSS method does not perform as well as previously reported for the western US.

we have demonstrated the difficulty of transferring methods to other ecosystems with different biophysical and ecological characteristics, but that the automated method can provide useful information on the spatial and temporal distribution of disturbance in Pacific Northwest forests.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the automated approach does not provide adequate accuracy for mapping forest disturbances in the Pacific Northwest.
automated LTSS classifications can be used for monitoring disturbance in Pacific Northwest forests but that the accuracy is not as high as in other ecosystems.
the spectral trajectory based image segmentation method is not robust enough to map forest change in Pacific Northwest forests and that the method should not be used in this region.
